frameworks.name: Talent ROI Framework
frameworks.definition: Calculate hiring investment by converting annual gross profit per specialized role into lifetime value, then benchmark recruitment spend as a percentage of that lifetime gross profit to determine hiring budget.

claims.text: Scaling service agencies is constrained by the trained talent bench available to service demand; adding high-value specialized roles generates compounding organizational value when recruiting investment is properly calculated (Hormozi, social media agency example at ~$12M revenue seeking to reach $25-30M).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Constraint is belief about hiring cost vs. actual unit economics, not feasibility; once the ROI math is visible, hiring becomes a capital allocation decision rather than an obstacle.
bounded_by: Applies to service businesses with repeatable, high-margin specialized roles
Does not apply to one-time or non-repeatable hiring needs

claims.text: For a specialized service role generating $1.25M annual gross profit, with ~4-year average tenure and 8x enterprise value multiple, acquiring that person adds $10M in enterprise value. At 20% net profit threshold, $125K recruiting spend to add $1.25M annual gross profit is sound capital allocation (Hormozi, on director-of-social example in social media agency).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Gross profit per role is $1.25M annually

numbers.axis: Investment to annual profit ratio for key hiring

bounded_by: Assumes profitable business (not applicable to pre-revenue or low-margin operations)
Assumes 4-year tenure baseline; shorter tenure reduces lifetime value

claims.text: The cost-to-acquire-a-person (CAT) equation mirrors customer LTV-to-CAC: lifetime gross profit per employee divided by cost of acquiring talent, just as customer revenue is divided by customer acquisition cost. This lens enables hiring discipline at scale (Hormozi).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Repeatable roles with measurable gross profit per employee
claims.mechanism: Treating hiring as an acquisition problem with a quantified ROI ratio creates the same capital-allocation discipline as marketing spend, preventing psychological bias against hiring investment.

claims.text: Specialized roles warrant premium recruiting spend; standard agency recruiting fees (~30% of annual salary, or $60K for a $200K director) are justified when the role's lifetime value exceeds 8-10x the recruiting fee (Hormozi, on blue-chip recruiting firm spend for specialized talent).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Specialized role with limited talent pool
High gross profit per employee (>$500K annual)
Repeatable future demand for this role
claims.mechanism: Premium recruiting fees are economically sound when the lifetime value (annual gross profit × tenure years) greatly exceeds the fee by an order of magnitude, turning recruiting as a cost into recruiting as an investment.

numbers.axis: Recruiting fee as percentage of annual salary and lifetime value multiple

anchors.region: Standard recruiting fee for specialized role
Example: Director of social at $200K salary
Minimum lifetime value multiple to justify spend

bounded_by: Does not apply to one-off hires or roles with short tenure expectations
Assumes access to quality recruiting firms

claims.text: Scaling a repeatable role (e.g., sales team, customer service, media team) justifies building end-to-end recruiting infrastructure; scaling a one-time role does not, and the founder should pay a flat recruiting fee instead (Hormozi, on infrastructure trade-offs).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: You have a clear repeatable role (sales, media, cleaning, etc.)
Multiple hires of the same role are planned over next 2+ years
claims.mechanism: Repeatable roles amortize the cost of recruiting infrastructure (process, team, relationships) across many hires, driving cost per hire down. One-off roles do not provide the volume needed to justify that infrastructure investment.
bounded_by: Does not apply if you will only hire for that role once
Infrastructure ROI assumes steady hiring cadence (not sporadic)

claims.text: To rapidly scale a specialized hiring need (50 people in 90 days), deploy 15+ parallel recruiting channels simultaneously (headhunting firms, internal assets) and expect 60% net hire rate (hire 80, keep 50), accepting that you'll oversample and filter (Hormozi, on building a 50-person sales team in 90 days).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Urgent scaling need (90 days or less)
Sufficient budget to pay recruiting firms and offer competitive comp
Role has some fungibility (sales roles, not unique specialists)
claims.mechanism: Saturation of multiple recruiting channels in parallel overwhelms scarcity constraints and creates competition for candidates, enabling rapid hiring velocity. Oversampling (hiring 60% above target) filters for retention and fit.

numbers.axis: Recruiting channel saturation and net hire rate

bounded_by: Assumes budget to support 80 hires (even if only 50 retained)
Effective only for roles that can be onboarded quickly
Does not apply to highly specialized roles requiring months of training

claims.text: Many founders fail to hire needed talent not because talent is unavailable but because they underestimate the cost required; they avoid hiring due to misalignment between perceived cost and actual ROI math, not because the economics don't work (Hormozi, on dentist example where 3 specialists would cost $300K but generate $3.7M profit).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Clear unit economics exist for the hire
Founder has done the lifetime value calculation
claims.mechanism: Hidden cost blindness causes founders to perceive recruiting spend as an expense burden rather than an investment with measurable ROI, leading to self-imposed scarcity that is psychological, not economic.

examples.text: A social media agency billing clients like Netflix, NBC Sports, Verizon, Visa, and State Farm generates $12M revenue and wants to reach $25-30M. The constraint is not market demand (four State Farm clients are available) but internal belief: when the team was asked how to acquire four State Farm clients in a year, they said it was impossible due to staffing limitations, even though the economics supported it. The team had not calculated the unit ROI per director-of-social hire ($1.25M annual gross profit per person with 4-year tenure = $5M lifetime value at 8x multiple = $10M enterprise value added).

A dental practice doing $20M revenue with $4M annual profit was constrained by specialized dentist availability. The owner believed acquiring three specialized dentists was cost-prohibitive. When the math was shown ($700K gross profit per dentist × 3 = $2.1M lifetime profit, with $100K recruiting spend per dentist = $300K total), the owner could pay $300K upfront to achieve his two-year goal in six months instead, accepting $3.7M profit this year instead of $4M. The constraint was belief, not economics.

A portfolio company needed to build a 50-person sales team in 90 days due to rapid business growth. The solution was to hire 80 salespeople total (60% net hire rate) using 15+ parallel recruiting channels (headhunting firms plus internal recruiting assets) operating simultaneously. This saturation approach enabled 50 good fits to be retained by filtering through the larger cohort and accepting hiring inefficiency as a trade-off for speed.

practices.text: When building a repeatable hiring process for a key role, map out the complete role definition, estimate gross profit per employee, and calculate the lifetime value (annual gross profit × expected tenure). Use this to set a recruiting budget as a percentage of lifetime value (typically 10% is justified for high-value specialized roles).

For one-off or non-repeatable hiring needs, do not build internal recruiting infrastructure; instead, negotiate a flat fee with a headhunting firm (typically 20-30% of annual salary) and pay it as a service purchase rather than an investment.

When facing a tight hiring deadline (weeks to months), activate multiple recruiting sources in parallel—headhunting firms, internal networks, LinkedIn recruiter, job boards—rather than relying on one sequential process. Plan to oversample (hire above your target) and filter for retention and fit.

Treat hiring spend as a capital-allocation decision using the lifetime-gross-profit-to-cost-of-acquiring-talent (LGPF/CAT) ratio, just as you would evaluate customer LTV-to-CAC. If the ratio is >5:1, the hire is economically sound regardless of the upfront spend.
